props.title: Willard

sections.content: Willard launched the "revenge of nature" horror subgenre that dominated 1970s creature features. Bruce Davison plays the socially awkward title character who befriends and trains an army of rats, using them to exact revenge on his tormentors. The film's success directly influenced Ben (1972), its immediate sequel, and paved the way for eco-horror hits like Frogs (1972) and Night of the Lepus (1972). The psychological depth of Willard's character transformation from meek outcast to vengeful mastermind set it apart from typical monster movies of the era.

sections.content: The 2003 remake starring Crispin Glover maintained the psychological horror elements while amplifying the dark comedy aspects. But the original Willard remains influential for its serious approach to human-animal relationships in horror. The film shares DNA with later works like Phenomena (1985) and Monkey Shines (1988), where isolated protagonists form dangerous bonds with animals that lead to violence. SUBHEAD: The Rise of Animal Horror

Willard emerged during a perfect storm of environmental awareness and post-60s cynicism. Films like Kingdom of the Spiders (1977) and Day of the Animals (1977) followed its template of nature-strikes-back narratives. The rat scenes were groundbreaking for their time, using hundreds of trained rodents rather than the rubber props common in lower-budget features. This authenticity influenced later animal horror films like Cujo (1983) and Anaconda (1997).
